topic.subject: science
topic.title: Living organisms and their surroundings
topic.scope: characteristics of living things, habitat, adaptation, biotic and abiotic components

nodes.name: Soil and Air as abiotic factors

misconceptions.statement: If an object does not move from one place to another, it is not alive.
misconceptions.why: Students observe animals moving but see plants as stationary objects.
misconceptions.fix: Plants are living things that do not move from place to place, but they show internal movements like water transport and opening of flowers.

probe.question: Is a mango tree alive even though it stays in the same spot for years?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it cannot walk or run like animals.

misconceptions.root_belief: visible movement is the only sign of life

misconceptions.statement: Clouds are living things because they grow in size.
misconceptions.why: Students associate any increase in size with the biological process of growth.
misconceptions.fix: Living things grow from within using food, whereas clouds increase in size by accumulating water vapor from the outside.

probe.question: Why is a growing cloud not considered a living organism?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it doesn't have a mouth, but it is still growing like a baby.

misconceptions.statement: Plants only respire at night when they are not photosynthesizing.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the gas exchange of photosynthesis with the continuous process of respiration.
misconceptions.fix: Respiration is a continuous process that happens in all living cells, including plants, both day and night.

probe.question: When do plants take in oxygen for energy?
probe.wrong_answer: Only at night, because during the day they only do photosynthesis.

misconceptions.root_belief: biological processes are synonymous with everyday actions
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Plants do not respond to stimuli because they don't have senses.
misconceptions.why: Plant responses are often slow or subtle compared to the quick reactions of animals.
misconceptions.fix: Plants respond to stimuli like light, gravity, and touch, such as a sunflower turning towards the sun.

probe.question: What happens when you place a potted plant near a window with sunlight?
probe.wrong_answer: It just sits there; it doesn't know where the sun is.

misconceptions.statement: Dry seeds are non-living objects until they are planted in soil.
misconceptions.why: Seeds in a packet show no visible signs of life like growth or movement.
misconceptions.fix: Seeds are living things in a dormant state; they carry out life processes very slowly until they find the right conditions to germinate.

probe.question: Is a moong seed in a jar alive or dead?
probe.wrong_answer: It is non-living because it is dry and not growing.

misconceptions.root_belief: dormancy is the same as death

misconceptions.statement: Abiotic factors like soil and air are just surroundings and not part of the habitat.
misconceptions.why: Students often focus only on the living residents when defining a 'home'.
misconceptions.fix: A habitat includes both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components that interact to support life.

probe.question: What makes up a pond habitat?
probe.wrong_answer: Just the fish, frogs, and plants living in the water.

misconceptions.statement: Camels store liquid water in their humps to survive in the desert.
misconceptions.why: The hump is a prominent storage-like structure and camels go long periods without drinking.
misconceptions.fix: The hump stores fat, which serves as a food reserve; camels conserve water by producing concentrated urine and not sweating.

probe.question: What is inside a camel's hump?
probe.wrong_answer: A large sac of water for the camel to drink later.

misconceptions.statement: If you move a desert plant to a mountain, it will grow thick fur to adapt immediately.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse adaptation (evolutionary) with the idea of an organism 'trying' to change.
misconceptions.fix: Adaptations are inherited features developed over thousands of years; an individual cannot change its physical structure to adapt to a new environment instantly.

probe.question: Can a single cactus change its shape to survive in a cold forest if moved today?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will change its leaves to stay warm.

misconceptions.root_belief: evolutionary change happens within a lifetime

misconceptions.statement: Plants do not excrete waste because they don't have a digestive system.
misconceptions.why: Students associate excretion only with animal-like waste removal.
misconceptions.fix: Plants excrete waste products through secretions, dropping old leaves, or storing wastes in vacuoles.

probe.question: How do plants get rid of unwanted materials?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't; they use everything they take in.

misconceptions.root_belief: humans/animals are the prototype for all life

misconceptions.statement: A piece of wood is an abiotic component because it is not moving or growing.
misconceptions.why: Students categorize anything that isn't currently alive as abiotic.
misconceptions.fix: Biotic components include living things and things that were once part of a living organism, like fallen leaves or wood.

probe.question: Is a fallen branch in a forest biotic or abiotic?
probe.wrong_answer: Abiotic, because it is dead and like a rock.

misconceptions.statement: Fish breathe by swallowing water and turning it into air in their stomachs.
misconceptions.why: Students see fish opening and closing their mouths constantly.
misconceptions.fix: Fish use gills to absorb oxygen dissolved in water; the water passes over the gills and out through slits.

probe.question: Why do fish constantly open their mouths?
probe.wrong_answer: To drink water so they can get air from it in their bellies.

misconceptions.statement: Cactus spines are only for protection against animals.
misconceptions.why: Spines look like needles, and needles are for protection.
misconceptions.fix: Cactus spines are actually modified leaves that reduce water loss by transpiration and also provide shade.

probe.question: Why does a cactus have spines instead of broad leaves?
probe.wrong_answer: Only to prick animals that try to eat them.
